report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister’s claim is supported—provided “cannabidiol” means the standardized, prescription purified product used *in addition to* existing antiseizure medicines, not over-the-counter CBD products.

The strongest evidence is two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in children/adolescents (and some young adults) with treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. In the first (120 participants; 14-week treatment), median monthly convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 with cannabidiol, versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo—an adjusted additional reduction of 22.8 percentage points.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618

A confirmatory dose-ranging trial randomized 199 children aged 2–18. Convulsive seizures decreased by 48.7% with 10 mg/kg/day and 45.7% with 20 mg/kg/day, compared with 26.9% on placebo. Thus, the benefit was replicated, although placebo response and individual variation were substantial.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458

This evidence underlies regulatory approval: the FDA label indicates prescription cannabidiol (Epidiolex) for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients aged ≥2 years. It is an add-on treatment, not a cure, and trials were relatively short, so they establish short-term seizure-frequency benefit rather than long-term developmental or mortality benefit.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/210365s023lbl.pdf

Important trade-offs include sleepiness, reduced appetite, diarrhea, fatigue, rash, infections, and liver-enzyme elevations; liver monitoring and attention to interactions (especially with clobazam and valproate) are needed. This should be managed by the child’s epilepsy specialist.
